verdict_reasoning: Reviewers agree the negotiated group is worth exposing, and the cost stays inside contrib/sslinfo. The shape of the result is not settled. demand-1 and maintenance-fit-3 show no use case for the shared and client supported rows, and the server's list cannot be fetched. standards-compat-1 and standards-compat-2 show that v7 ships an undocumented helper function and an empty result that has several meanings. Nobody has replied to v7.

brief.title: Add ssl_group_info() to contrib/sslinfo to show TLS key exchange groups
brief.problem: The sslinfo extension shows the cipher and protocol version of the current connection but not the TLS group used for key exchange. The author wants this for TLS diagnostics and debugging, for example to see which key share was negotiated, such as X25519MLKEM768 on newer OpenSSL.
brief.proposed_design: The patch adds a set-returning function ssl_group_info() to sslinfo version 1.3, with one row per group and a group_type of negotiated, shared or client supported. v7 adds ssl_group_info_with_nulls(), which returns null rows when no group was negotiated, and ssl_group_info() wraps it and filters the nulls out. Build checks in configure and meson detect the OpenSSL group functions, and the function returns no rows when they are missing.
user_visible_surface: New function ssl_group_info() returns setof record, with columns group_type and name.
New function ssl_group_info_with_nulls(), which v7 adds as the base for ssl_group_info().
group_type values: negotiated, shared, client supported.
sslinfo extension version bumped to 1.3 through sslinfo--1.2--1.3.sql.
New configure and meson checks for OpenSSL group functions in pg_config.h.in.
author_claims: The function helps diagnose which key share the client and server negotiate.
The sslinfo scope has grown beyond certificates before, so adding handshake facts is acceptable if documented.
Builds whose OpenSSL lacks the group functions, such as 1.1.1w, still compile, and the function returns no rows.
The implementation follows ssl_print_groups from OpenSSL.
brief.thread_state: Gustafsson, Champion, Huang, Parragi and Si reviewed it, and v7 says it addresses the comments, but nobody has replied to v7 yet. Champion and Si doubt the value of the non-negotiated rows, and the naming, the error on unknown group names and the silent skip on old OpenSSL were still open.
unclear: The material does not say what v7 returns when there is no negotiated group under RSA or non-EC DHE key exchange with TLSv1.2 or older.
The material does not say whether v7 still raises an error when SSL_group_to_name() returns NULL for a group the server does not know.
The material does not say whether the docs mention the empty result on OpenSSL builds without the group functions.
The documentation hunk does not describe ssl_group_info_with_nulls().
The server's own group list is missing, and the author says OpenSSL has no public API for it.
The thread did not settle whether the shared and client supported rows are worth keeping next to the negotiated group.

objections.title: Row-type layout fixed before the wider handshake-info design is settled
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch exposes ciphersuites or signature algorithms with the same negotiated/shared/supported pattern. It must either copy this group_type vocabulary, with its OpenSSL-derived names and no server row, or add a different shape next to it. sslinfo then has two styles that users must correlate.
objections.argument: In message #8, Champion asked whether this table is how future negotiated parameters should look, and noted the missing server side. Message #9 answers 'I don't see why not', but the server list cannot be fetched (no public OpenSSL API), and 'shared' is not a TLS term. Champion and Si (messages #6, #17) doubt the non-negotiated rows. A single ssl_group() scalar, like ssl_cipher(), would commit the project to less.
objections.author_must_show: If ssl_group() returned only the negotiated group like ssl_cipher(), what diagnostic case would still need the shared and client supported rows?

critic.reasoning: Message #9 answers Champion's question about the table shape with "I don't see why not" and gives no design. The server list is still missing, and Champion and Si both doubt the non-negotiated rows.

objections.title: ssl_group_info_with_nulls() becomes a permanent, undocumented part of sslinfo 1.3
objections.failure_scenario: A user finds ssl_group_info_with_nulls() through \dx+ sslinfo and uses it in a monitoring query. A later release wants to drop or change it and needs a new extension version, which breaks that query. Both an RSA connection and an unknown client group produce a null row, so neither user nor maintainer can tell them apart.
objections.argument: Message #18 adds the function as an internal way around SRF limits, but every function in an extension script is user-callable API. The documentation hunk does not describe it, and no other sslinfo function follows a "_with_nulls" naming pattern. Message #21 maps the unknown-name case of message #20 onto the same null rows, so two different facts look the same after filtering. A committer would likely ask for one function whose result states the absent or unknown group directly.
objections.author_must_show: Can a single documented ssl_group_info() return explicit rows, such as a null name or an 'unknown (0x...)' name, so that no helper function ships?

critic.reasoning: Message #18 adds the helper function to the extension script, and the v7 documentation hunk does not describe it. Message #21 maps the unknown-name case onto the same null rows, so the two cases look the same.

objections.title: Same sslinfo 1.3 returns an empty set on builds without group functions
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA runs ssl_group_info() on a package built against OpenSSL 1.1.1 and gets zero rows. They read this as no key exchange group, or a non-TLS connection. Nothing tells them the build lacks the API, and the same query returns rows on another server running the same extension version.
objections.argument: Message #20 asked for diagnostics for the silent skip, and message #21 answered a different point. The documentation hunk does not mention build-dependent results. Other build-dependent features usually report "not supported by this build" when called. A committer would likely want an error, or at least a documented and distinguishable result, before calling the contract stable.
objections.author_must_show: Why should a build without the OpenSSL group API return an empty set instead of raising a feature-not-supported error?

critic.reasoning: Message #20 asked for documentation or diagnostics for the skip, and message #21 answers only the unknown-name point. The v7 documentation hunk does not mention the empty result on builds without the group functions.

objections.title: No shown demand for the shared and client supported rows
objections.failure_scenario: An administrator asks why a client did not use X25519MLKEM768 and gets the client supported and shared lists, but not the server's list, so the question stays open. The project still has to keep the three group_type values, their names and their meaning stable in every later sslinfo version.
objections.argument: The only use case given for the non-negotiated rows is the author's own experiments (messages #1, #5), and message #9 says the work began only to get the negotiated group. Champion says he uses other tools for TLS debugging and suggests server-side debug logging (message #6), and Si doubts the rows (message #17). No field report or user request in the material asks for these lists. Without the server side, which message #9 says OpenSSL cannot expose, the lists cannot explain a negotiation result.
objections.author_must_show: Which users have needed the shared or client supported lists from SQL, and what question could they answer with them that openssl s_client or server logs cannot?

critic.reasoning: Message #9 says the work began only to get the negotiated group, and the thread shows no user request for the other rows. Champion and Si both question them, and the author's reply gives no diagnostic case.

refuted.title: group_type text values are a fixed contract that is not yet settled
refuted.failure_scenario: Users write where group_type = 'client supported'. A later patch adds the server side of the list (message #8), or renames the values to TLS terms, and these filters stop matching rows after upgrade without any error.
refuted.argument: Message #8 asked for names from the TLS specification or names clear to non-experts. Message #9 says "shared" and "negotiated" come from OpenSSL documentation, and message #17 questioned "supported". v7 uses "client supported", a value with a space, which is unusual for an enumerated text column. Message #8 also asked whether this table shape would serve a later ciphersuite view, and the thread has no answer.
refuted.author_must_show: Which group_type values would stay unchanged if a server-side list or a matching ciphersuite function is added later?

critic.reasoning: A new server-side value would not stop an existing filter on 'client supported' from matching, and no one in the thread proposes a rename after v7. The open design question about the table shape is covered by maintenance-fit-3.

refuted.title: Version-dependent OpenSSL API added to top-level configure for one contrib function
refuted.failure_scenario: A packager builds against OpenSSL 1.1.1 or LibreSSL, and the build passes. A DBA there calls ssl_group_info() during a TLS incident and gets zero rows with no notice, so it looks as if no group was negotiated. The next OpenSSL or LibreSSL release that changes macro-versus-function status breaks the check, and the buildfarm finds it after commit.
refuted.argument: The patch adds decl checks for SSL_get1_groups and SSL_get_negotiated_group to configure, meson.build and pg_config.h.in. Message #12 notes that some of these are macros and some are functions. The check was wrong in v5 (message #15), and the meson placement was wrong in v6 (message #20). sslinfo had two reverts for this exact reason, use of functions that older OpenSSL or LibreSSL lacked [P4][P17]. Message #20 asked about the silent empty result, and the visible v7 docs do not mention it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which OpenSSL and LibreSSL versions on the buildfarm were tested, and how does a user on a build without these functions tell 'unsupported' from 'no group'?

precedents.title: Revert "Add notBefore and notAfter to SSL cert info display"
Revert "Add notBefore and notAfter to SSL cert info display"

critic.reasoning: P4 and P17 were reverted for lacking compatibility checks, which this patch adds, and Postgres already probes OpenSSL functions in configure and meson. The silent empty result is a duplicate of standards-compat-2, and the future macro change is speculation.

refuted.title: ssl_group_info_with_nulls() makes an implementation detail a permanent SQL API
refuted.failure_scenario: After 1.3 ships, users start calling ssl_group_info_with_nulls() directly, since it is installed but not documented. Its null-row behaviour then becomes a contract. A later redesign cannot drop or change it without another extension version and an upgrade script, so the project keeps two functions where one would do.
refuted.argument: Message #18 adds the second function only because the SRF code path cannot skip a row. A C-level SRF can loop past NID_undef internally, so the extra SQL object exists only to work around that code path. The v7 documentation hunk does not describe ssl_group_info_with_nulls() at all. Every function in an extension script stays in the catalog until a later version removes it on purpose.
refuted.author_must_show: Why can ssl_group_info() not skip NID_undef or unknown groups in C, so that only one function is installed?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. Its point that a C set-returning function can advance past an entry before returning a row is correct and supports that objection.

refuted.title: Client supported and shared group rows repeat what a handshake capture shows
refuted.failure_scenario: An administrator debugging a key-exchange choice runs ssl_group_info() and gets the client-offered and shared lists. A packet capture of the cleartext ClientHello and ServerHello already shows the same lists. sslinfo must still keep three group_type labels, their naming and the OpenSSL build checks stable for what is mostly a convenience view.
refuted.argument: The supported_groups extension and the key_share are sent in clear text, so tshark or Wireshark on a Postgres connection already show the client list and the chosen group. `openssl s_client -starttls postgres` also lets an administrator test which group the server picks. Message #9 says the author only needed the negotiated group, and messages #6 and #17 doubt the other rows. The negotiated group matches ssl_cipher() and has the strongest case for SQL access.
refuted.author_must_show: Which diagnostic task needs the client supported and shared rows from SQL, when a capture of the cleartext handshake already shows them?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1, which makes the same point about the shared and client supported rows with better support from the thread. The packet capture alternative can be raised under that objection.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: sslinfo 1.3 adds two SQL functions that stay installed until a later extension version removes them.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: ssl_group_info_with_nulls() becomes a permanent, undocumented part of sslinfo 1.3

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The function reports TLS handshake facts, limited to the caller's own connection.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-2: Same sslinfo 1.3 returns an empty set on builds without group functions

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: New configure and meson checks for OpenSSL group functions, plus fixed group_type values and a helper function.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Reviewers in messages #6 and #17 doubt that the shared and client supported rows belong in SQL.

questions: Which diagnostic task needs the shared and client supported rows from SQL, given that the server's own group list is not available?
Why not ship a scalar ssl_group() that returns only the negotiated group, like ssl_cipher(), and add the lists later if users ask?
Can ssl_group_info() skip or label missing groups in C, so that ssl_group_info_with_nulls() is not installed?
How does a user tell apart no negotiated group, an unknown group name, and a build without the OpenSSL group functions?
If ciphersuites or signature algorithms are exposed later, will they use the same group_type table shape and values?

committability.owner_note: Daniel Gustafsson reviewed in message #2 and handled the earlier sslinfo reverts (P4, P17). The owner needs to know the OpenSSL and LibreSSL build matrix.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the build checks on every supported OpenSSL and LibreSSL version, and for the function names and group_type values, for as long as sslinfo 1.3 is installed anywhere.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted seven versions in response to review and moved the entry between CommitFests, which suggests continued follow-up.

priority.reason: The patch is about 15 KiB, confined to contrib/sslinfo and build checks, and serves people who debug TLS key exchange. The function set and result shape need agreement before another review round is useful.

provisional_note: Without the code, I could not check what v7 returns for RSA or non-EC DHE key exchange, or whether it still raises an error for an unknown group name. The build checks on LibreSSL and old OpenSSL were also not verified.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

instead of its own test suite.  There are too many complications that we

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallel grouping sets
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add parallel execution of GROUPING SETS queries by splitting aggregation into partial and final stages, first by grouping on the union of all grouping columns in workers and doing the grouping-sets aggregation in the leader. The later version instead performs grouping-sets aggregation in workers, tags each partial tuple with a grouping set ID, and has the leader combine results per grouping set, with refactoring of nodeAgg.c (phase reorganisation, sorting inside the Agg node).
precedents_retrieved.objection: The last patch version received no review and no longer applied to HEAD. A PGCon hallway-track discussion of the approach concluded that nodeAgg.c needs refactoring before it is complicated further, and after an off-list discussion with Melanie, who had picked up the patch, the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There was also considerable discussion in a (virtual) hallway-track session
during PGCon which reviewed the approach (for lack of a better description),
deeming that nodeAgg.c needs a refactoring before complicating it further.

precedents_retrieved.title: remove_useless_groupby_columns is too enthusiastic
precedents_retrieved.summary: Change remove_useless_groupby_columns so that it no longer removes GROUP BY items that are functionally dependent on a primary key when those items also appear in ORDER BY. This keeps the link between the GROUP BY and ORDER BY lists, so the planner can use a sorted index path with GroupAggregate and avoid an explicit sort.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers pointed out that keeping the redundant columns can make plans worse. Without a matching index, the extra sort columns cost more (Richard Guo measured a slowdown). Hash Aggregate would always pay for hashing and comparing the extra columns. David Rowley proposed a different design: mark redundant GROUP BY columns instead of removing them, and consider both the full and the minimal key sets. No revised patch followed, and the entry was marked Returned with Feedback after the thread had been idle for some weeks following that review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So the
patch makes that case worse in favour of possibly making Group
Aggregate cases better.

precedents_retrieved.title: group locking
precedents_retrieved.summary: Robert Haas proposed a heavyweight-lock concept of "locking groups" for parallelism: a user backend and its worker backends would form a group whose lock requests never conflict with each other, with changes to lock acquisition, wait-queue handling and the deadlock detector so that no group member waits behind an unrelated process. The posted patch was an incomplete draft (LockAcquireExtended() and ProcSleep() modified, ProcWakeup() and the deadlock detector not) meant to get feedback on the design.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the leader could hold the locks for its workers, and that the proposal added too much complexity, with bugs and performance costs, to the lock manager. Andres Freund objected that letting group members hold self-exclusive locks at the same time removes guarantees that existing code relies on, citing transaction abort (smgrDoPendingDeletes) and relcache invalidation. Robert Haas then dropped the original design because it would put too much coordination burden on the workers, and moved to granting the leader's existing locks to workers at the start of a parallel operation. The visible thread ends without agreement on that alternative or a revised patch, and the closing decision is not shown.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Based on your arguments and those of others, I have long-since abandoned the original proposal of having locks within a group never conflict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Indeterminate behavior for the GROUP BY clause
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Indeterminate behavior for the GROUP BY clause
Section: Features We Do Not Want
Linked: Re: SQL compatibility reminder: MySQL vs PostgreSQL
precedents_retrieved.objection: At least one other database product allows specification of a subset of the result columns which GROUP BY would need to be able to provide predictable results; the server is free to return any value from the group. This is not viewed as a desirable feature. PostgreSQL 9.1 allows result columns that are not referenced by GROUP BY if a primary key for the same table is referenced in GROUP BY.

precedents_retrieved.title: Collecting statistics about contents of JSONB columns
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a jsonb_typanalyze function that extracts every path from sampled JSONB documents and stores per-path statistics as an array of JSONB documents in pg_statistic under a new stakind. It also adds an "oprstat" procedure for operators such as ->> so the planner can derive statistics for expressions on JSONB columns.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tests showed ANALYZE becoming much slower: about 28 seconds against 120 ms on one data set, and over 2 hours or OOM on documents with about 850k distinct paths, because the patch loops over all sample rows once per path. The reviewers agreed the design of collecting statistics for every path in every JSONB column needs rethinking, for example by keeping only the most common paths or enabling the statistics per column. Nikita Glukhov posted optimizations and planned common-path collection, but in the last week of the commitfest the patch no longer applied and Greg Stark asked for a rebase.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: From these points, we can say that we should rethink our design to collect stats for all paths.

precedents_retrieved.title: When deleting the plpgsql function, release the CachedPlan of the function
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Matthias van de Meent, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch frees the CachedPlan contexts of a PL/pgSQL function or procedure when DROP FUNCTION or DROP PROCEDURE runs, so they no longer stay in CacheMemoryContext until the session ends. The author showed with pg_get_backend_memory_contexts() that a dropped and recreated procedure leaves two sets of CachedPlan contexts.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch frees cached plans only in the backend that runs the DROP, because other sessions do not execute RemoveFunctionById and keep their plans. Tom Lane suggested that PL/pgSQL, or funccache.c so SQL functions also benefit, install a shared-cache-invalidation callback on pg_proc that marks function trees as deletable. The author agreed, linked a new thread, and withdrew this entry. Vladlen Popolitov also asked why the plans should be freed at all.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It doesn't, which is (one reason) why it's just a crude hack.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add sslmode "no-clientcert" to avoid auth failure in md5/scram connections
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a new libpq sslmode value, "no-clientcert", that makes libpq ignore the default client certificate and key in ~/.postgresql/. A user with those files could then still connect with password authentication to servers that do not know the certificate.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch because Jacob Champion's separate patchset adds sslcertmode=disable, which already stops libpq from sending a client certificate. Reviewers found that option the more elegant way to get the same result. Jelte Fennema also pointed out that setting sslcert to a file that does not exist already works around the problem.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm withdrawing this patch, as the same feature was already implemented
in a different patch written by Jacob[1]

roaster_notes.note: No earlier attempt at this idea is in the list. P4 and P17 are two reverts of other sslinfo functions, caused by missing OpenSSL or LibreSSL functions. This patch answers that risk with build-time checks, so the only check left is a buildfarm run on LibreSSL and old OpenSSL. The thread does not mention any earlier discussion of exposing TLS groups.
P4 and P17 were reverts over OpenSSL and LibreSSL build breaks. This patch adds configure and meson checks, so those recorded reasons do not apply directly.

The proposal holds no persistent or cross-node state. It adds functions that read the TLS state of the current backend's connection, with no WAL, on-disk, wire protocol or core catalog change. The 1.2 to 1.3 upgrade script follows normal extension practice, and v7 no longer touches libpq-be.h.

No security objection. ssl_group_info() reports only the current connection's own handshake facts, the same scope as ssl_cipher() and ssl_version(). It shows nothing about other sessions, server memory or files. The error on an unknown group name affects only the calling session. Precedents [P4] and [P17] are OpenSSL portability reverts with no privilege aspect, so they belong to another angle.
The change is confined to sslinfo and costs nothing for non-users. The objections concern build-matrix upkeep and the permanent SQL surface.
The negotiated group is not exposed today by ssl_cipher(), pg_stat_ssl or connection logging, so that part has no existing alternative.

Demand for the negotiated group itself is reasonable: Champion and Si want it next to ssl_cipher() (messages #4, #17), and Huang supports the extension (message #13). The cost stays inside contrib/sslinfo.
